cards.prompt: You need a chatbot to draft a short thank-you email to a client who helped with a project. Which prompt will get the most useful first draft?

options.text: "Thank-you email to Sam, a client who helped us finish early. Friendly, under 100 words"
"Please could you write a really lovely, thoughtful and professional thank-you email?"
"Write a thank-you email. Make it as long and detailed as you can, with lots of examples"
"Write a thank-you email to a client", with the temperature turned right up for variety

cards.explanation: Only the first prompt gives the **goal** (a thank-you email), the **context** (who Sam is, what they did) and the **format** (friendly, under 100 words). Being polite, asking for length, or turning up the temperature doesn't tell it who the email is for or what to say.

cards.prompt: "Make a list of healthy snacks." What would improve this prompt **most**?

options.text: Saying who they're for and how many you want
Asking for lots of detail and plenty of examples
Asking it to include only snacks that are healthy
Turning the temperature up for more variety

cards.explanation: It has a goal but no context (for a lunchbox? a 12-year-old?) or format (how many?). More detail, repeating "healthy", or a higher temperature don't add either.

cards.prompt: Sort these bits of prompts: the **goal**, the **context** or the **format**?

items.label: I'm 12 and it's for a science test
Here are my notes from class

cards.explanation: The **goal** is what to do; the **context** is who it's for and what you already have (your age, your notes); the **format** is the shape and length.

cards.prompt: A chatbot helping with a bake sale says: "You have 5 trays with 8 cupcakes on each, so that's **45** cupcakes." Check it. How many cupcakes are there really?
cards.explanation: 5 × 8 = **40**, not 45. A likely-looking number isn't always right, so check sums yourself.

cards.prompt: A chatbot says there are **about 50** kinds of penguin, with a link to a zoo's website.

steps.text: The link opens a real zoo page about penguins. What now?

choices.text: It's checked: the page is real
choices.consequence: A real page isn't proof. Read whether it says the same thing.

choices.text: Read the page to see what it says
choices.consequence: The page says there are about 18 kinds of penguin.
Asking the chatbot doesn't check anything.

steps.text: You tell the chatbot the page says about 18. It replies: "Sorry, you're right, it's 17." Which number do you use?

choices.consequence: Right: go with the source you actually read, not the chatbot's new guess.
Its "fix" is just another guess. The page says 18.

cards.explanation: Open sources **and read them**, then go with what the source says. A chatbot's correction is just another prediction.

cards.prompt: A chatbot (that can't search the web) says a band's newest album came out "this year". What's the main risk?

options.text: It may have mixed this band up with another band's album
Chatbots can't handle dates, so every year they give is a random guess
It learned up to a certain date, so "this year" may be out of date
Its temperature was set too high, so it picked a random year

cards.explanation: Without web search, a model only knows what it learned up to a certain date, so "this year" and "newest" may be long out of date. Mix-ups can happen too, but that's the main risk here.

cards.prompt: It's late, and you're stuck on one question in tomorrow's maths homework.

steps.text: You open a chatbot. What do you ask it?

choices.text: Explain the method with a different example, then try mine myself
choices.consequence: It walks through a similar question, and you work out yours. You did the thinking, so you've learned it.

choices.text: Give me the answer, and I'll write it out in my own words
choices.consequence: Rewriting its answer doesn't change who did the thinking. It's still the chatbot's work, and you haven't learned the method.

choices.text: Give me the answer and the working, so I can copy it neatly
choices.consequence: You'd hand in its work as yours, and you'd still be stuck on the test. Ask it to help you learn instead.

cards.explanation: Using AI to **learn** (explaining a method, then trying it yourself) is great. Getting it to **do the work**, even if you reword it, isn't, and many schools have rules about it.

cards.prompt: You're 14. A new AI chat app's rules say users must be **18 or older**. All your friends are using it. What's the best move?

options.text: Don't sign up yet: talk to a parent or carer about it
Ask a friend who's 18 to sign up and share their account
Sign up, but never upload any photos of yourself
Sign up anyway: lots of people your age already use it

cards.explanation: Each app sets its own rules about who can use it. If an app says 18+, it isn't for you yet, whatever friends do, and using someone else's account still breaks the rules. **Check the rules and ask a parent or carer**; some apps do allow younger users with a parent's OK.
